references.text: In Matthew's parallel account, Jesus strictly commands the disciples not to tell anyone that he is the Messiah, which directly corresponds to Luke 9:21.
Mark's parallel account where Jesus forbids the disciples from telling anyone about him after Peter confesses him as the Christ.
Jesus did not allow the evil spirits to speak because they knew who he was. This shows the same pattern where Jesus commands silence regarding his identity.
Jesus strictly commanded the unclean spirits not to make him known, another example of Jesus' command for silence concerning his messianic identity.
Jesus commanded the leper not to tell anyone, an earlier example in Luke of Jesus commanding silence after a revelation of his power.
After raising Jairus' daughter, Jesus commanded the parents not to tell anyone what had happened, a similar injunction to keep it secret.
After the transfiguration on the mountain, Jesus commands the disciples not to tell anyone about the vision until the Son of Man has risen from the dead, showing that the secrecy was temporary.
Jesus withdrew because the crowd wanted to make him king by force. This clarifies why Jesus wished to keep his messianic identity hidden—to avoid misunderstood messianic expectations.
